title: The Press and the Protest
paragraphs: It is tempting to tell the story of the Reformation as a simple chain of cause and effect: a new machine appeared, and a religious revolution followed. Johannes Gutenberg's system of movable metal type, developed in Mainz in the middle of the fifteenth century, certainly made texts cheaper and far quicker to reproduce than copying by hand. Yet the Church was among the early customers of the new presses, and among the earliest dated printed items, attributed to Gutenberg's press, were letters of indulgence, the very documents whose sale would later provoke Martin Luther.

When Luther set out his Ninety-five Theses in 1517, he wrote them in Latin as propositions for academic debate. Tradition holds that he posted them on a church door in Wittenberg, although historians still disagree about whether that scene took place. What is far less disputed is that printers soon reproduced the theses, and that Luther went on to write short pamphlets in German, which could reach readers well beyond the universities.

A comparison sharpens the point. A century earlier, the Czech reformer Jan Hus had raised criticisms of the Church that resembled Luther's in several respects, and he was burned at the stake in 1415. His ideas survived in Bohemia, but without presses they travelled slowly. Printing did not create the grievances; it changed how quickly they could circulate and how difficult they were to suppress.

Historians nonetheless disagree about how much weight the press deserves. Elizabeth Eisenstein argued in 1979 that print was a genuine agent of change, while her critics warned against treating technology as destiny, arguing that print mostly carried messages shaped by wider social forces. The more defensible view is that printing was a necessary condition for the speed of the Reformation rather than a sufficient explanation for it.

sources.claim: Johannes Gutenberg hareketli metal harfle baskıyı 15. yüzyılın ortasında Mainz'da geliştirdi; baskı makinesine atfedilen en eski tarihli basılı öğeler arasında endülijans mektupları vardır.
Luther Doksan Beş Tez'i 1517'de Latince, akademik tartışma önermeleri olarak yazdı; Wittenberg kilise kapısına asıldığı geleneği tarihçilerce tartışılır; tezler kısa sürede basılıp yayıldı.
Luther sonraki yıllarda geniş okur kitlesine ulaşan Almanca broşürler yazdı.
Çek reformcu Jan Hus Kilise'yi eleştirdi (endülijanslar dahil) ve 1415'te Konstanz'da kazıkta yakıldı.
Elizabeth Eisenstein 1979'da matbaayı bir değişim etkeni olarak ele alan eserini yayımladı; bu tez tarihçiler arasında tartışılmıştır.
sources.source: Elizabeth L. Eisenstein, The Printing Press as an Agent of Change, Cambridge University Press (1979)
